title: Lagaan Returns to Theaters for Its 25th Anniversary. For the Diaspora, It's a Homecoming of a Different Kind.
excerpt: Aamir Khan's Oscar-nominated cricket epic gets a three-day re-release on June 12, a new trailer, and a poster challenge that invites fans to reimagine the film that changed how the world saw Indian cinema.
body:
In the summer of 2001, a village called Champaner did what no Indian film had managed before it. It made American Oscar voters care about cricket. Twenty-five years later, Lagaan is coming back to theaters — and for the millions of Indians who watched it while building lives in other countries, the timing feels less like marketing and more like memory.

Aamir Khan Productions announced this week that Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India will return to cinemas on June 12, 13, and 14 for a special three-day theatrical run. A new anniversary trailer has already dropped, reassembling the film's most visceral moments — the parched fields, the colonial sneer, the impossible cricket match, and A.R. Rahman's music swelling underneath all of it.

## The Film That Traveled

What made Lagaan unusual wasn't just that it earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Foreign Language Film. It was that it arrived at a moment when Indian cinema was invisible to the global mainstream. There was no pan-India release strategy, no IMAX window, no day-and-date international rollout. Lagaan traveled because audiences carried it — in suitcases of VHS tapes, in weekend screenings at rented community halls, in word-of-mouth that crossed oceans before social media existed.

For NRIs in their twenties and thirties at the time, the film was a cultural event that had nothing to do with Bollywood's usual formula. It was a period film about taxation and cricket and dignity, directed by Ashutosh Gowariker and starring an actor who had spent years being difficult about scripts. That it worked at all was improbable. That it became a generational touchstone is the part worth celebrating.

## A Poster Challenge and a Cast Reunion

To mark the anniversary, Aamir Khan and Gowariker have launched the #LagaanPosterChallenge, inviting fans to reimagine the film's iconic promotional artwork. The best submissions earn an invitation to a special anniversary screening with the original cast and crew. Entries can be submitted via email at lagaanposterchallenge@gmail.com or shared on Facebook, Instagram, and X.

The campaign is characteristically understated for a film that was anything but. Lagaan's original ensemble — Gracy Singh as Gauri, Paul Blackthorne as the contemptuous Captain Russell, Rachel Shelley as Elizabeth, Raghubir Yadav, Rajesh Vivek, and the rest of the village cricket squad — remains one of the most memorable casts in Hindi cinema. Several of the actors never appeared in another film of comparable scale. They didn't need to. Lagaan was enough.

## Why the Diaspora Angle Is Personal

There is a generation of Indian Americans, British Indians, and Canadian Indians for whom Lagaan was the first film they could show their non-Indian friends without a long preamble about song-and-dance conventions. The cricket match in the third act plays like a sports movie regardless of whether you understand the LBW rule. The colonialism is specific enough to be Indian and universal enough to land anywhere.

That generation now has children old enough to watch the film on their own. The re-release offers something streaming cannot: the communal experience of watching Bhuvan's team assemble in a darkened theater, with an audience that knows the ending and still holds its breath.

## A.R. Rahman's Score, 25 Years On

The soundtrack deserves its own paragraph. Rahman's work on Lagaan — "Ghanan Ghanan," "Mitwa," "Radha Kaise Na Jale," "O Rey Chhori" — was composed before he became a two-time Oscar winner. It was composed before he became the name that Hollywood called when it wanted India. Listening to it now, the ambition is obvious. This was a composer writing music for a period drama set in 1893, using instruments and vocal textures that had no business working together, and making them sound inevitable.

## The Road Ahead: Aamir and Gowariker Reunite

The re-release also carries a forward-looking footnote. Reports confirmed in late May that Aamir Khan and Ashutosh Gowariker are reuniting for a new period sports drama based on the life of Lala Amarnath, India's first Test centurion, set against the 1952 India-Pakistan series during the Partition era. Rajkumar Hirani and writer Abhijat Joshi are reportedly involved in the screenplay. Shooting is expected to begin in October 2026.

It is, in some ways, the obvious next chapter: the director and star who made cricket feel like revolution taking on the true story of a man who used cricket to bridge a political wound. For the diaspora, particularly those whose families were shaped by Partition, the subject matter carries a weight that goes beyond sports.

But that film is still a year away. For now, there's Champaner. June 12, in a theater near you — if you're lucky enough to find one screening it.
